utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner assisted by Crispian Smith, Case Manager, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence this morning, Igor Pantelic, Dragan Krgovic, and Miroslav Cuskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour instructed us yesterday that we should give our position on two outstanding motions. And I informed the usher that whatever pleases the Court I can do it right now while the witness is ushered in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, we do not object to -- to safe conduct motion. To the safe conduct granted to the witness; and the second thing was the protective measures. It is our understanding that the protective measures have been already granted in a previous cases for two, and for -- for the third one which was asked by the Prosecution we do not object, so therefore ... Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We don't have objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Korner, I don't know whether you have been alerted that you have 46 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I knew that yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Before Ms. Korner resumes her questioning of you, I would remind you that you're still on your oath. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Skipina, I only have 45 minutes left to question you, so I would be grateful if we could move fairly quickly through the remaining matters. Yesterday you mentioned when you were answering questions from Judge Harhoff, and this is at page 8339 of the transcript, a man called Batko who committed, as you put it, misdeeds against the Bosniak people in Grbavica, in Sarajevo. Do you remember mentioning him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you said to the -- the -- the Judge, I think that, Mr. Planojevic had told you that the minister knew about it and that he took it upon himself to inform the army about it, because Batko was a member of the Territorial Defence? Was Batko ever arrested during this period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was ever arrested, but I know that this: After a while, when that question was raised, he disappeared, vanished from that area, and nobody knew where he went. Whether any steps had been taken, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Has he been recently arrested?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard he was arrested in Spain.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... matter of a month or so ago; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I suppose that's him, because I didn't know his last name, but I think it's him but his nickname. It was said he had committed crimes at Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he had been arrested as a result of a warrant from the Bosnia State Court; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what his orders -- or warrant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. One other matter, you talked about the building in Pale in which you were housed whilst you were head of the SNB. Was that a building known as Kalovita Brda?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a small administrative building of the scouts union at Kalovita Brda.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is it right that the various government buildings in Pale are all fairly close to this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All of them are at least 1 kilometre away from that building.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Whilst you were in charge of the SNB, did you receive reports from military intelligence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I received from time to time reports of the military security service, their intelligence section. I'm not aware of their organisation internally. And these small reports would be addressed by the army to the President of the Republic, the Speaker of the Assembly, the prime minister, and my name would also be there, as head of the National Security Service. I'm not sure if it was copied to the minister of the interior as well because I occasionally briefed Minister Stanisic about the substance of these military reports. But they usually concerned the military situation, the situation on the battlefield, where they were doing well, where they were in jeopardy. Nothing particularly important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But did you actually have meetings with Colonel Tolimir, as he then was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first met Colonel Tolimir towards the end of May when he came to occupy a leading position in the Army of Republika Srpska together with General Mladic. He came to my office to introduce himself. We talked very briefly. He described briefly the situation in the theatre of war in Croatia where he had come from, and after that, I met him another three or four times, but we did not speak at length.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And, finally, on the question of personnel, before I turn to the various meetings you went to, did Dragan Devedlaka that you mentioned, who appears on the chart, did he become, for a short period, before he went off to Belgrade, the chief of the CSB in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Do you want to know the background how that came about?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just deal with some specific questions about that. He was one of your subordinates. Was it you who appointed him as chief?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who made the appointment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it was the minister, but I can only suppose. I can't be sure. The thing is, I sent Dragan Devedlaka as my deputy to Bijeljina to check whether there were any operatives of the State Security Service who had fled from Tuzla and to find them, rally them, give them basic instructions about work and to see who among them could be head of sector of the State Security in the process of forming a Security Services Centre. We needed a head of the state security sector who could approve of candidates, and Dragan Devedlaka really went to Bijeljina and spent there about ten days, and then I expected he would come back. But then I received a fax message saying that Dragan Devedlaka was appointed head of the CSB. Namely, there were some problems in the area of Semberija. There were two candidates for head of centre, one was Jesuric and another one was someone named Cvjetinovic, but the politicians could not agree which of them would get the appointment so the vacancy remained for quite some time. My assumption is that the authorities from Bijeljina could not have appointed Dragan Devedlaka because they didn't know him. Therefore, I suppose it was done by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, didn't the fax tell you that? As it was -- he had been appointed by the minister?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I tried to explain in my first interview with the OTP, that I did not quite understand this. I only remember from that fax message that Dragan Devedlaka was appointed head of the Security Services Centre. I can really not be sure any longer who signed the fax message, but that's what it said. I just deduced that it could have been Minister Stanisic who appointed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, because it's a long time since you listened to your interview, can I just remind you at page 44 of the interview that what you told the OTP was that a fax came stating that Dragan Devedlaka, with the approval of the Minister of the Interior, Mico Stanisic, was appointed the head of the CSB in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just a moment, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Korner. We lost the LiveNote, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh. Yes, we've all lost it, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The technician is on his way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We are advised that this is a -- not peculiar to this courtroom. The whole system has a problem which may take, quote/unquote, several minutes, so we'll rise until it is repaired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 9.27 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the purposes of the record, Ms. Tatjana Savic has joined the Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Skipina, when we had to adjourn I just read to you what you said in interview about the fax; namely, that it had been said that Devedlaka, with the approval of the minister of the interior, was appointed the head of the CSB. Is that right, what you said in interview?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. All right. I want to move now fairly swiftly through some of the meetings that you told us about. First of all, on the 12th of May, not really a meeting as such, but did Mico Stanisic tell you that he was going to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell me he was going to Banja Luka, but I heard in conversations that he had been to Banja Luka to attend a promotion ceremony of the police of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. When you way "promotion ceremony," what do you mean? A parade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a ceremony to promote the police force with new insignias, as opposed to the old police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you know how he got to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, did you explain to -- when you were interviewed about how he got to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I explained how the minister got to Banja Luka, but I did explain how, on one occasion, I had asked the minister that if anyone should be travelling by helicopter to Krajina because no other way was possible, to get me a place on that helicopter so I can go to Banja Luka and visit the National Security Sector. However, that never happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, I believe the witness said the military helicopter. I think it might be important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you say "military helicopter," sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, military helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware of the special unit of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the special police led by Milenko Karisik at Vrace? Yes, yes, I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did that have any helicopters?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the special police had helicopters that, allegedly, and I heard this from Vlastimir Kusmuk, who was in charge of the police, helicopters that were broken and needed to be sent for repair and were transported one to Serbia and one to Greece. There were two helicopters. So throughout the war, or, rather, as long as I was head of that service, the special police or the MUP, at least as far as Sarajevo was concerned, did not have any helicopters because I know that when a policeman was injured he had to be transported by car. There were no helicopters in operation in the region of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the special police unit that operated out of Banja Luka attached to the CSB there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You sound very positive about that, sir. All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am -- I'm really very positive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move then, please, to the 1st or about the 1st of June. Did you pay a visit to Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the orders of Minister Stanisic, I and assistant minister for the police, Vlastimir Kusmuk, went to Trebinje. Because the minister had told us that certain problems had cropped up in the relations between the employees of -- of the CSB and other security personnel. Let me just remind you that in mid-April I sent Novak Blagojevic to Trebinje to try to rally together the operatives who had fled from Mostar to Trebinje. And after seven days, Blagojevic returned and he had the same instructions as Devedlaka, by the way. He told me he had been expelled from Herzegovina by some MPs and some employees of the CSB. He didn't name any names, but he said people from the CSB because before the war he had worked in that area on Serb nationalism.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry to stop you, sir, but I'm afraid because of the limited time I just want to know - if anyone wants to ask you further questions they can - I simply want to know about your meeting -- the meeting that you and Mr. Kusmuk had with Krsto Savic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were attending the meeting. That was my first visit to Trebinje and before the meeting I went to the offices where the National Security Service employees were. There were three employees, one active duty, and two of them retired. I asked them what they were up to. They said basically nothing. They said Krsto Savic had told them that they would only be working when he issues them orders but they said basically he kept them idle. Two employees, Ljubisa Traparic to the best of my recollections, and Miro Prelo, were forbidden access to these offices because they, too, before the war, as employees of the State Security Service, had been engaged in work concerning Serb nationalism. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Please, just tell us about the conversation that you and Mr. Kusmuk had with Krsto Savic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that meeting of the senior staff of the CSB, I also saw Jovo Cokorla, a former employee of the State Security Service, with whom I was collaborating before the war. I was an inspector at the Republic level, and he was an inspector at the lower level. And I said, Let's appoint Jovo Cokorla head of sector for national security. And I got the answer, He's still being vetted as to whether he is a good enough Serb. Then his commander took the floor and said, Nobody's -- we're not going to have anyone from the outside making appointments in the National Security Service. We are going to decide on these matters ourselves. And the only ones who are going to be admitted are those who have proven themselves in the fight against Bosniaks, Muslims. And I had to react. I said, As long as I'm head of this service, such people will not be working in this service, and you are not going make any appointments in the service, and that's how the meeting ended. And that's the first time that I told Vlastimir Kusmuk that I was going to resign because I can't get along with people like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you said that Cokorla should be appointed as head of the sector, who gave you the answer, He's still being vetted as to whether he is a good enough Serb?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krsto Savic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From Trebinje did you go on to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't go to Bijeljina. But sometime during those days, and I can't pin-point the date, those two meetings in Trebinje and in Bijeljina took place within a short interval. It was a long time ago, so I can't even tell which one took place first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause. I'm going ask you again, please, sir, specific, questions, and I would be grateful if you just concentrate on the questions rather than telling me the whole story. Who asked you go to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did he explain why he wanted you to go to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Briefly tell us why he wanted you to go.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said there would be a meeting tomorrow in Bijeljina, a meeting of the political leadership of Semberija, which includes Bijeljina, Ugljevik, Lopar, Zvornik, and other municipalities that belonged to Semberija. The two of you will be going to attend that meeting. You don't have to speak, just be there and listen. After that meeting, conduct interviews with Mirko Blagojevic, leader or President of the Serbian Radical Party in Bijeljina, and Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer and tell them or, rather, convey to them my order and the order of the President of the Republic that they should place themselves under the command of the army and stop mistreating Bosniak citizens in Bijeljina and leave police work to the police station in Bijeljina, the public security station in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask when you recalled, please, for the first time that in addition to saying that these two people should put themselves under the command of the army that Mico Stanisic had also added that they must stop mistreating Bosniak citizens?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the question, When I recalled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because as you remember, when you were interviewed you didn't mention that last part about Mico Stanisic saying that they should stop mistreating Bosniaks. So I'm just asking when it was that you first remembered that part of the interview. Or, sorry, the conversation with Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I mentioned that to the investigators the first time they interviewed me. At least that's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I will be corrected if I'm wrong, this is page 59 of your interview. That part of the interview, that part of what you just said did not appear. However, let's move on. So can you just briefly tell the Court, please, first of all, what it was that Blagojevic and Ljubisa Savic were doing towards the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting, which was attended by around 30 persons, the first one to take the floor was a lieutenant-colonel, whose name I don't remember, who had been on the battlefield in -- at Majevica, an area bordering on Tuzla. He said he was short of troops, that his lines were as hollow as Swiss cheese whereas Bijeljina was full of soldiers --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop. Sorry, that is not the question about the meeting. The question was, what was it that Blagojevic and Ljubisa Savic were doing to make Mico Stanisic, you say, say they should stop mistreating Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that meeting Vlastimir Kusmuk and I had separate discussions with Blagojevic and with Ljubisa Savic, also known as Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, stop for a moment, please, and concentrate on the question. You say that Mico Stanisic said you should speak to Blagojevic and Savic, Mauzer, to say they should stop mistreating the Bosniaks. Before the meeting, before you spoke to them, what did you understand from Mico Stanisic or anybody else they were actually doing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I concluded something based on what I was told by the minister. I didn't want to make any assumptions of my own, at least not before speaking to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... all right. Can you tell us exactly what the minister said to you that these two men were doing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeated to them that they should stop mistreating the Muslims in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sure you did. I'm not interested at the moment in what you said to Savic and Blagojevic. I'm interested and I'm asking you what the minister told you that these two men were doing before you ever went to Bijeljina with Kusmuk.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing else. I was only told that we should discuss things with Mirko Blagojevic and Ljubisa Savic, aka Mauzer, telling them that they should put themselves under control of the army and to stop mistreating the citizen of Muslim ethnicity. There were no other explanations, save for that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But unless you knew what it was they were doing from Mico Stanisic, how were you going to tell them to stop doing it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, we were tasked to speak to them, to hear them out as well, to see what they had to say of each other, and we did so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. How did Mico Stanisic know that these two people were mistreating Muslims? Did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how he knew. I did not tell him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And so you didn't ask for any other further details before you spoke to these two men about what it was they were doing towards Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You told us you spoke to these two men. And what happened?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the chief of the public security station, whose name I believe was Pantic, we asked that Blagojevic and Savic be summoned to the station so that we would have an opportunity to speak to them. I think Mirko Blagojevic was the first one to appear. When we put questions to him about the problems, he told us that Ljubisa Savic, aka Mauzer, had a unit of his own, comprising only Serb refugees who had fled from Tuzla, Gradacac, and elsewhere. He also said that Ljubisa Savic, aka Mauzer, was expelling Muslims from their homes in Bijeljina in order to find accommodation for the fighters of his unit. That was the gist of what Blagojevic told us. When we spoke to Ljubisa Savic, aka Mauzer, he said that Mirko Blagojevic's unit was cruising Bijeljina trying to protect Muslims, and those of them who were well off, paid to his unit to be transferred abroad, via Serbia. What he said was basically that they had business of their own running -- up and running with the Muslims. That's what Ljubisa Savic said about Mirko Blagojevic. After these conversations, we conveyed to them the orders of Mr. Stanisic and the President of the Republic, but I don't think it had much effect. Later on, they resumed in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did Mico Stanisic give you instructions as to what you should say to them, if they wouldn't agree?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He probably said something else, but I can't be sure. It's been a while. I only remember the main points. I don't really remember whether he said that they would have problems because of that or not. Please do bear in mind that it's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You have got a fairly good memory about him saying that you should speak to them and that you should tell them that they should stop mistreating Muslims. If they didn't stop mistreating Muslims, what was to be the sanction? Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't. This would entail further assumptions. I only wanted to share with you the task we were assigned and how we carried it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why was it that this was something within Mico Stanisic's area of responsibility? In other words, that he should instruct you to tell these men to stop mistreating Muslims. Why was it his job?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose because, in some way, they took over control of the town of Bijeljina instead of the public security station. It was my presumption that Aco who was the chief of the station complained to him stating that the station was unable to function because of them. It basically became clear later. They prevented the MUP from doing their work. They were doing things of their own in Bijeljina pressuring the MUP to leave saying that they had no need of them. There were quite a number of issues with those units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you report back to Mico Stanisic the results of your conversation with the two men?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Any task issued by Minister Stanisic was something that he would be briefed on later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... at this same meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just ask if I have understood the witness's testimony correctly. Because from your question it would appear and from the witness's testimony that Minister Stanisic had ordered you to get hold of Blagojevic and Savic and tell them to stop mistreating Muslims. And then when you got hold of Savic, he appeared to have told you that Blagojevic was having his own unit that was cruising Bijeljina, and I'm now quoting from what you have just told us, "trying to protect Muslims, and those of them who were well off, paid to his unit to be transferred abroad." So I'm just a bit confused, what was it that Savic told you that Blagojevic was doing? I mean, because it appears that he was actually protecting Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it is a protection racket, rather, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But let's just be clear about what was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That Blagojevic was actually supposed to have done. That is unclear to me. Can you clarify, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were the very words of Ljubisa Savic. That's what he said about Mirko Blagojevic. This is not something I said. Ljubisa Savic said, Blagojevic's men were not engaged in fighting the war. They were simply going about town taking money from the Muslims and transferring those among them who were rich elsewhere. That's what Savic said about Blagojevic. That's what he had to say about him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. But my question is then: Did that correspond to what Minister Stanisic had told you about the activities of Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Basically it was contrary to what Stanisic had told us about them mistreating them. He said that both were mistreating the Muslims, and this was contrary to what Ljubisa Savic had to say about Mirko Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what did you make out of it then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my conclusion that they both had interests of their own to stay in the town and not go to the front lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Korner. I'm terribly sorry. The part of the answer -- the witness's answer previously, it is page 16 from line 20 until 17 -- page 17 line 2, the part of his answer was not recorded where he was -- he was saying that these people were threatening the -- the MUP when it moved into the Bijeljina and they were against that and -- I just -- I just thought maybe this could be clarified with the witness. I'm sorry, Ms. Korner but.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 16, line 20 starts with, "I suppose because, in some way, they were -- they took over control of the town of Bijeljina instead of the public security station" and then on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "It was my presumption that" the name of the chief of the station "complained to him stating that the station was unable to function because of them. It basically became clear later." What is missing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because -- because the context is lost because what he -- what he -- what the witness tried to -- to establish that it became clear later when the MUP was set up -- its headquarters in Bijeljina they were protesting about it, and they wanted the MUP to go away from Bijeljina. Well, that was -- that is the gist of what I wanted you to clarify with the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Skipina, you have heard what Mr. Zecevic said. Is this right, that, later on, when the MUP was being established in Bijeljina, these men protested? Blagojevic and Savic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. They never accepted the fact that the MUP headquarters was supposed to come to Bijeljina from Pale. They kept saying we'd have no need of you. Can you go up to the hills, and we'll deal with our problems here ourselves. That was the gist of it. They never basically accepted that the seat of the MUP be in Bijeljina. In my view, it indicated to me that they had much more -- much more space to manoeuvre before the MUP came than afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just to make it absolutely clear, that was the period when the headquarters of the MUP moved from Pale to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, at that same meeting, and I'm afraid we really need to take this very quickly, and I have got three documents I need you to deal with as well. And in Bijeljina, did you come across a man called Goran Zugic who you had known before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the expanded meeting, Goran Zugic participated as well who was an employee of the Tuzla security service. I did not approach him during the meeting itself. It was only later that I asked him what he was doing there. And he said he had fled Tuzla in early May and since then was in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. Okay. He was in Zvornik. And did he tell you about what was happening in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him about what the news were in Zvornik. He said that in Zvornik there was a strong paramilitary unit called "Zute Ose," yellow wasps. He said that they basically looted all of Zvornik including the Glinica factory and that they used trains to ship the goods to Serbia. He also said that they had committed crimes of -- over Muslims. He also said that he was in contact with Minister Stanisic and that he tasked him with, to the extent possible, checking who the members of that group are and whether they had any links to the municipal leadership, what their base was, and so on. Upon my return to Pale, I and Kusmuk informed the minister of the contents of the meeting and the discussions with Blagojevic and Mauzer. I also told him that I met Goran Zugic. The minister then said, Yes, I had given him some tasks, although he didn't explain which. He also said that it concerned a large group comprising criminals from Zvornik and its environs as well as from Serbia. He also said something to the effect that he would have to arrest them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to -- Goran Zugic after the action which followed, although I don't know much about it, received threats that he would be killed. He fled to Montenegro because of that. For a while, he worked with the MUP in Podgorica and Herceg-Novi. I think it is important to say that he was killed while he was security assistant to Mile Djukanovic, the Montenegrin president. He was killed in front of his apartment, which may have been a result of the threats he had received while in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Anything may have happened. But, look, all I want to know is this: Did either Zugic or Mico Stanisic explain to you how they had been in contact with each other without going through you as head of the National Security Service?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither of them explained. The minister, as the man number one, had the right to issue individual tasks without having to explain it to anyone. Perhaps it would have been fair to inform that individual's superior that he was doing something for the minister so that the immediate superior would know that his employee had been issued a task by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But, you see, you told the Court yesterday that you had received no reports of these crimes that were being committed against Muslims as head of the State Security Service. So does that mean you didn't know anything about what was happening in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything. I didn't know that Goran Zugic was in Zvornik, and we had no communication. I didn't know anything about the crimes in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the minister knew about them. And the minister knew about the crimes in Bijeljina, but you knew nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I did not have a service up and running in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you simply have no idea how it was that Goran Zugic had got in touch with Mico Stanisic to tell him about these crimes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no idea. I suppose once Goran fled, he reported to the minister and received tasks from him, but I had no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And this meeting with Goran Zugic took place at the same time as the Bijeljina meeting which was at the beginning -- sometime around the beginning of June 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him for the first time at that meeting in Bijeljina. The people working in Bijeljina knew him because --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... don't worry about that. I just want the date. It's around beginning of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I have to move really quickly through the remainder, please, of the matters that I want you to deal with. You told us that it was your meeting with Savic that led you to say to Kusmuk you were going to resign. Did you, in fact, resign at the beginning of July?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we have a very quick look at the resignation letters that you sent to Mr. Stanisic and, indeed, Mr. Djeric. Your Honours, it's -- the letters themselves aren't important so I'm just putting them up -- they're not part of our document list. It is just to remind him. 10324. It's the mere fact of his resignation as opposed to the -- to the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll see the English in a minute, I hope. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that the letter that you wrote to Mico Stanisic on the -- it's dated 3rd of July, saying that you were resigning and the reason you gave for the resignation was that you were being mentioned in the media as one of the main culprits in criminal activities. And you were asking effectively for your culpability be ascertained and you have also informed the prime minister, Mr. Djeric, of this. And I don't think we need bother with that. And you told us yesterday that it was at the time of your resignation that you had the meeting with Mr. Djeric where you talked about the various crimes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But the term "crimes" is not fully applicable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to waste too much time on this. But what you say is fully applicable.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat the answer, it was unintelligible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, you have to repeat your answer, Mr. Skipina. Interpreters didn't hear you. What's the applicable word, if not "crimes."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Different types of criminal offences. Crime can be one aspect of criminal conduct directed against civilians, et cetera, but there are other types of criminal offences directed at property as well as people, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You resigned. I'd like you to look, please, at a record of a meeting held on the 6th of July, which is -- it's P168.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While that document is coming up, Ms. Korner, how much longer do you think you would be?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've got three -- I'm literally just going to rush him through these documents. Have I finished my time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Notwithstanding the lengthy break we had with the technical problems, I still intend do take a break this morning because the accused would have been in court during that period, and I was thinking that I would -- I was looking at the clock and thinking that it would have been convenient for you to finish and then we take the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is literally three -- three -- no four documents but I'm just going to literally ask him to identify that he was at that these meetings and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If you say ten minutes then perhaps we better take the break now and then --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it's the length of time it takes to come up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, to save time, while the witness is coming in, could I have up the document that I was asking for, which is P168. And it's page 20 in English, and page 20 in B/C/S. English? No. One in English and one in B/C/S, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skipina, when we adjourned, I was about to ask you to look at this document, which is a record in somebody's diary of a meeting apparently in Trebinje on the 6th of July, so three days after your resignation. And it appears that you were there together with your travelling companion, who seems to be around the place most of time, Mr. Kusmuk, also Mr. Draskovic, and Mr. Vukovic, and Krsto Savic was there again. Do you recall three days after your resignation because, as we will see, you did stay with the MUP, that you attended this meeting in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this meeting, nor do I remember being in Trebinje after submitting my resignation. I was in Trebinje just twice, once during the tenure of Minister Stanisic, the second time during the tenure of Minister Ratko Adzic. I saw here on one document, 20-something June. It could have been before and in some other place. I quite simply am not aware of this meeting. It's impossible for me to recollect that I was in Trebinje after resigning. After submitting my resignation, I never went into my office again. I sat outside my office. If any of the operative officers asked me about anything, I directed him to Minister Stanisic and that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, but Mr. Stanisic, as we'll see, kept you on as a special advisor, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As of 6 August.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but -- are you saying that at no stage, this is what you're saying, that whoever compiled this record has got this completely wrong, that at no stage did you attend a meeting in Trebinje with Mr. Kusmuk and Mr. Draskovic and an inspector called Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Trebinje. Maybe somewhere else. But whoever wrote this record, if you have the details I'm not saying that this meeting never took place, but it's just that I can't remember it at all. It couldn't have been on the 6th of July, because all the time, from my resignation, I was with Minister Stanisic on the 4th, with Minister Djeric on the 3rd. I never went into the offices again. I simply couldn't have attended this meeting. Whoever wrote this record should tell us where this meeting took place, but with 99 per cent certainty, I can say it was not in Trebinje. Maybe 1 per cent I can write-off -- I can put down to my bad memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember a meeting, wherever it was held, but attended by the people shown there where there was a discussion and you apparently spoke as well about the formation of separate police units at the level of the centre ... and then Mr. Draskovic talking about a special-purpose unit.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anywhere in the text that I spoke about separate police units. I could have only spoken about things concerning the National Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I haven't got enough time to pursue this further. Even though you had resigned, you did attend the 11th of July meeting, didn't you, in Belgrade? I don't want to ask you anything about the detail, but you were there, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And, as you say, on the 6th of August --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we have up, please, document 2382, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You received an official appointment. And is that your appointment?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, we haven't got the English get.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So, in fact, although you had officially resigned your position as head of the SNB, you never actually left the MUP, did you, because between July and 6th of August, when you got your formal appointment, you were still part of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was part of the MUP, but I wasn't doing anything, and I can explain further, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No thank you. I don't need you to explain further. And I should have ask you this. I think it's right that you were replaced as head of the SNB by Dragan Kijac. Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not immediately. Kijac and Dragisa Mihic managed the service together for a while after my resignation. And on 6th of August, the minister appointed Kijac head of the service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And then I want to finally deal quickly with two other meetings that you attended. On 9th of September, I think you attended the steering council meeting of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up, please, document 00239. Your Honours, although the last document is on our list, again, I don't see that it needs to be exhibited, unless anybody wants it. Well, it's on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what is the position. We don't object that this document be just for the accuracy of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay, I'm happy. In that case, Your Honour, may I ask that the appointment of Mr. Skipina, in August, be -- become an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What's the 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did I say? It's 2382.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. One other thing, I don't know if -- if his resignation has been exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It wasn't on our 65 ter. I can -- I can exhibit it, if I'm allowed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For continuity and completeness, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. That was my idea, because.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. In that case, that is, please, 10324. I'm just waiting for exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay. This would be exhibit -- so 65 ter 2382 becomes Exhibit P1267; and 10324 becomes Exhibit P1268, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Do we there see the record of the meeting on the 9th of September in Mount Jahorina? And we can see listed there advisors to the minister, and it's the, if I can put it, the terrible trio again, yourself, Mr. Kusmuk, and Mr. Draskovic. And do you remember attending this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was there for a short time, but I don't understand about the trio.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Forget that, I shouldn't have said that. It's just that you appeared together at the last meeting and you're together at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in that case, I don't have time to go through the contents, but could that be marked -- exhibited and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P1269, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, finally, the meeting of the 5th of November. And that is document number 266 [sic], another steering council meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, was this a meeting held in Bijeljina, which you attended -- attended as the minister's advisor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can see from the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we also see that although he didn't seem to attend the last meeting, on this occasion, Stojan Zupljanin was also there. Is that right? Do you remember seeing Stojan Zupljanin there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw Stojan Zupljanin before the session of the collegium that was held in Belgrade around - what was it? - 13 July or perhaps 11 July. That was the first time I met Stojan Zupljanin. Since this is the 5th of November, this was perhaps my third time seeing Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Because, in fact, in September, didn't you go to Banja Luka together with Kijac and have a meeting with Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But it wasn't a meeting with Zupljanin. It was a meeting with Kesic, and we only came by out of courtesy to greet the chief of the centre, have coffee with him, and then we moved to Kesic's office to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked then, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skipina, that's all --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P1270, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what was the 65 ter number? I didn't get that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Mr. Skipina. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Skipina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we changed the order of our examination because my examination will be very brief, in view of the witness's testimony. Mr. Cvijetic will question this witness after me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Mr. Skipina, let me introduce myself formally now, although we saw each other briefly last Sunday. I am Dragan Krgovic, and, on behalf of Stojan Zupljanin's Defence, I will ask you a few questions pertaining to your evidence. Since we speak the same language, there is a danger of overlapping, and, therefore, please make a short pause after each of my questions before you start answering to have a clear transcript. I will also take care, because I'm usually the source of the problem. Mr. Skipina, in your evidence, you spoke about your beginning in the National Security Service and your prior work. My question is: In view of all the circumstances that prevailed when the MUP of Republika Srpska was established and when you started to work, these circumstances were not regular. They were not normal.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And practically your service as the whole MUP of Republika Srpska was in its cradle you were just beginning to recruit personnel and establish separate services?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I explained that to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Small wonder, then, that there was not enough information, not enough exchange between different services in those early days, when the MUP was only starting to operate.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There is one particular fact pertaining to your service, namely, that for a long time, you did not have any contact with centres in Banja Luka, in Trebinje, and in some other places, because of a breakdown in communications.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were only CSBs in Banja Luka and Doboj that had operated even before the war. With them, I had no communication; whereas, with centres in Trebinje, Sarajevo, in Bijeljina, they were formed only later after the war broke out. But I have to emphasise that the sectors of national security in Trebinje and Bijeljina were not established even until the end of my tenure, except the sector in Sarajevo that was led by Dragan Kijac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And as you said in the interview to the OTP, you first met some managers, some senior staff of the centre at that meeting in Belgrade, in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the first time I met Andrija Bjelosevic, chief of the CSB in Doboj. Stojan Zupljanin, chief of the Banja Luka CSB; Predrag Jesuric; Nedeljko Kesic; and there were other chiefs of public security sectors perhaps Duro Bulic among them whom I also met then for the first time. Many senior officers whom I met for the first time then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also showed you a number of documents, and this is a slightly different topic regarding those daily bulletins, some of them bore your signature, others didn't. And you spoke about the style in which those documents were written. When you said the style was unusual, did you mean to say that it was not the normal style for your service? Your service did not write such documents in that way. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Our documents were more articulate, more concise. These daily bulletins contained certain things that are not really acceptable to me as a member of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On the other hand, from what -- from my understanding of the way the MUP operates, these were documents emanating from the operative duty service, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. In fact, I believe that the first information from the ground would come in to the operative duty officers who forwarded them to the analysis department, which summarized the information and put it together in the form of a bulletin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And an operative duty officer would just sum up the reports of operative duty officers from different centres and put them together in a single report, and that's the kind of bulletin that was shown to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, an operative duty officer will not take responsibility either for the style or grammar or contents. They wouldn't dare to change anything and the way they come in, they put it in the bulletin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And since this department for analysis was not really manned for a long time, this operative duty officer would put this information together on his own and just forward it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I signed them as such. Although, now, when I look at them carefully, perhaps I shouldn't have put my signature on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the style of this writing in the bulletins, that was the language that was normally in use at that time between the warring sides.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was common. And it's unbelievable how individuals started a new jargon that, until then, had not been acceptable, had not been in use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But in wartime, it was common, and that was so throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But, as I said, it's so unbelievable that both people and language can change so suddenly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that's the style and the expressions that all the three warring sides in Bosnia and Herzegovina commonly used.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. If you were there to -- to hear the conversations of Bosniak and Serb policemen through talkie-walkies you would be aghast at the terms they used on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In response to some questions from the Prosecutor in the last session, you spoke about the meeting of the 11th of July where you said you first met Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up, please, P160.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have some hard copies for you, with the usher's assistance. If it is easier for you to look at the documents on paper, I prepared a binder. Mr. Skipina, look at this document. I believe the Prosecution showed it to you during your interviews. Have you had occasion to see it before? It's your tab 1.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The title of the document is: Brief survey of the functioning of the MUP so far and the outline of future activities. It refers to a meeting of the senior staff of the MUP of 11 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When I say that it's a summary, it's an extract from the discussion from the deliberations at that meeting. It's the contributions and discussion that has been recorded. It's not a reflection of the entire meeting. It's just a summary. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A summary implies brief extracts from the broader discussion that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In e-court too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We can see the list of participants, including your name. Then look at the third paragraph from the top, which reads that the minister explained the method of work, made an introductory speech about the security situation and the role of organs for internal affairs, and then the chiefs of centres spoke about the security situation in the region and the tasks to follow. Does -- is this consistent with your recollection of the meeting, that the minister spoke first, made an introduction, and then the chiefs of centres spoke about the situation in their regions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe the minister opened the meeting and outlined the topics that would be discussed. He said that finally after three months we managed to meet all together, that it's important to make reports about the previous period and outline the problems we encountered, to see how we were going to work in the future, that we would make appropriate conclusions that everyone would have to abide by in the future. That was basically the introduction made by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the sequence of -- of the contributions to the discussion in which order the speakers took the floor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. According to this document, Mr. Zupljanin spoke second, which is possible, but I can't really remember. But if the document says so, and if this summary really reflects the sequence of the speakers, then Stojan Zupljanin came second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the document it also stated that the National Security Service will hold a separate meeting, but there are no conclusions from that meeting included in this summary; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I can explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps not. I'm only interested in the fact that this summary was merely an excerpt and is not a reflection of the entire meeting. That was the crux of my argument. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I have already said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But what did you want to explain? Perhaps we should allow you to do that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, there was a break after the contributions by centre representatives. There were four of us, as far as I can remember. It was myself, Kijac Dragan, Kesic, and Dusan Zivkovic from Doboj had a discussion group concerning the National Security Service. We did so separately, and I presume it is for that reason that it was not included in the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you met Stojan Zupljanin for the first time then. The Prosecutor asked you about that -- Stojan Zupljanin's contribution from the way you explained it in your interview. Could you please go to page 5 of the document, which is 8 in the English. Mr. Skipina, as far as I understand, there were several items, or topics which dominated the meeting, as you explained in your interview. First of all, most of the representatives of the centres complained about the work of the Crisis Staffs. Wasn't that one of the main topics at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you this. Those chiefs of centres basically addressed the same issues. There seems to have been a pattern. They all pointed out problems which they encountered in their work which were almost identical. Among other things, Crisis Staffs were mentioned as well as municipal leaderships, which tried to influence the work of the MUP and the public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And basically this is what you also mentioned in one of your answers to the Prosecutor when you said that those public security stations were under a lot -- a lot of influence exerted upon them by local leaders. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When answering Madam Prosecutor's questions, I said that the Ministry of Interior, on the 1st of April, inherited, so to speak, a lot of personnel which had been appointed in 1991 and who came there as party representatives without the necessary background and experience they should have possessed as chiefs of public security stations. They made use of that opportunity and in order to stress that they had been prosecuted -- persecuted in the past as political dissidents although some of them were actually from a criminal milieu they basically did not feel themselves to be part of the organs of the interior. They were in this vicious circle including municipal leaderships and to them it seemed that it was all that mattered, that they listened to their instructions and that the MUP was something very distant. At least that's how -- what my impression was of certain public security stations although not all of them, by no means. I didn't get to see all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, page 5, we see Stojan Zupljanin's contribution. He says -- he mentions the army and Crisis Staffs as well as War Presidencies which required that as many Muslims be assembled as possible and they did not leave such tasks to the Ministry of the Interior. He states then in the Assembly centres the conditions are poor and that they did not meet international standards. He also states that such centres were inadequate for different reasons. I presume this was the first time you heard of the existence of such centres and the poor conditions there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard for the first time of the existence of collection centres and camps from Stojan Zupljanin. I think he was the only one who mentioned that at the meeting out of all those here, including the chiefs of the centres. I didn't go through the whole document and all of the contributions because I simply wanted to preserve the -- my own memory, to see what I actually remembered. I believe he said that there were certain issues in the field with the existence of collection centres or camps, I'm not sure which term he used. I believe them to be the same. I couldn't tell a difference. In any case, he pointed out that there were such places, and as far as I remember, he mentioned the infamous -- yes, Omarska, the Omarska camp in Prijedor. I don't think he mentioned any others which does not mean there weren't any others. But as far as I remember, he referred to Prijedor and Omarska specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And basically he is saying that the army and Crisis Staffs were those detaining people in such centres. At least that's the way I read his contribution; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one would say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: A chief of CSB cannot deal with the issues concerning army alone. In a way, he had to inform his superior so that that superior would deal with that problem on a higher level; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was the intention of the meeting - and I believe it was - and if Minister Stanisic, in his introductory remarks said that he wanted to know from them what the problems were and how to overcome them, in order to continue working, he wanted to make certain conclusions, and I believe it was the duty of those centre chiefs to inform him of the problems they encountered. They had to inform their superiors, and, in this particular case, the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The issue of the army and their role in the establishment of those centres and detention, that is something that should have been dealt with by the government and Presidency as well as the Supreme Command. Is it not correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, all of them, or at least some of those bodies, rather than the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The role of the Crisis Staffs and their competences was something that needed to be dealt with by civilian authorities, the Assembly, and the Presidency, as well as the government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I also explained in one instance what the Crisis Staffs were doing. If they sent me 2- or 300 Bosniaks to Pale, then you can only imagine how they went about their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Stojan Zupljanin took the measures he thought were necessary. He wanted the minister to know so that issues could be addressed. What would you have done in his place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he pointed out the problems he encountered in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there were conclusions made at this meeting and that certain measures were taken following those conclusions in order to disband such centres and in order to establish what the situation was with them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the minister said that certain tasks would be issued after the meeting that everyone needed to abide by. However, I never saw those conclusions, not until 2004, when they were shown to me by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skipina, have a look at your tab 5, which is the last document, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 2D26 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you have occasion to see this document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not had a chance to see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know any of the persons mentioned here? This is a decision by which Stojan Zupljanin established a commission which was to visit the municipalities and public security stations of Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Bosanski Novi. Do you know any of the people mentioned therein?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I know the first two people, Bera, Vojin; and Vaso Skondric. Vojin Bera was a member of the National Security Service before the war. He was charge of a department in the state security centre in Banja Luka. Vaso Skondric worked in Sarajevo. I think he was a commander with the traffic police. As for the other two, I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You can see that there was a task by which the commission was charged with ascertaining whether there any remaining detainees and detention centres in the aforementioned municipalities as well as whether any citizens were being brought in and for what reason, as well as their numbers. He also wanted to know what the number of those processed was and what their age, ethnicity, and sex was, as well as the conditions of detention. Basically this seems to be a result of the conclusions of the 11th of July meeting and discussions held there.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the explanation, in the statement of reasons, it is stated what these tasks were derived from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We can see in the statement of reasons that --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That it was pursuant to the order of the Ministry of Interior ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It seems that something was done following the discussion and conclusions of the meeting in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to P160.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The first document in your binder; page 5 in the Serbian and 8 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 5 in the Serbian and 8 in the English. The number of the page is 03241855. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Another topic which dominated the meeting was the participation of policemen in military operations. The chiefs complained that the army took basically all police personnel in order to make them part of their operations, leaving the towns and settlements without any security bodies and that the MUP was unable to exercise its duties. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several chief who complained that they could not go about their activities the way they wished to because they were short of staff and that it had an impact on the increase of crime in their areas because they did not have a sufficient number of policemen who would work on the prevention of such crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 4 from the top, this is Zupljanin's contribution, the second sentence: The army wishes to engage the entire staff bringing the policemen to the battle-field and front lines. This was a serious issue that was discussed at that meeting, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that from my personal knowledge, but it seems that this was what Mr. Zupljanin's contribution was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Another issue that was discussed was the financing of MUP from a single source. If you look at the penultimate paragraph, where it says: "The financing of the MUP and of other services is the task of the Krajina Serb Autonomous District government, and when single funding is secured there will be fewer interventions and tempering?" Do you recall that as a problem, that the municipal authorities which financed such stations and military units also sought ways to influence the work of the MUP as well as its leadership?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a well-known rule, the person paying you is who you work for, and that's how it was. All centre chiefs complained of this problem of financing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There was also a mention made of the functioning of the communications system. Mr. Zupljanin said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat this part of his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreters need --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. [Interpretation] I apologise. I seem to have been too quick without waiting for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: One of the issues discussed at the meeting was the issue of communication -- communications. Mr. Zupljanin, in the last paragraph of his contribution, says that the functional system of communication was broken, that it broke down. Is this what you tried to explain when you addressed the system of communication within the MUP at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it broke down because, for example, I, who was at the helm of the National Security Service, did not have my communications system. What was communication like within the public security system and the means they could use in different periods of time is not something I'm fully familiar with, but I could overhear from time to time that the lines were down. I am no communications expert, hence, I cannot tell you anything specifically about what did and what did not function at what time. I only know that everyone was saying that the basic lines of communication concerning information went through Sarajevo and that this should be avoided until such time when there is an independent communications system in Republika Srpska. I know that apparently Minister Nedeljko Lajic, who was the telecommunications minister, perhaps in May, said, Now we have a complete communications system, but I'm not familiar what that system was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Turn the page, please. It's page 6 in B/C/S and page 9 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There were also complaints about the work of the military authorities, and it was said that the military prosecutor's office is not functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It says the military prosecutor's office is not functioning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will counsel please slow down. This can't be read this fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember hearing that there was discussion to the effect that the military prosecutor's office was not functioning?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not only the military by also the civilian prosecutor's offices. It was said they practically don't exist. They don't work. Everybody was saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have to go back to one topic. When we were saying that the functional communications system had collapsed, you said there was a problem with rounding off the telecommunications system, and Minister Lajic said something like, This system should be complete in May, but as long as you were on that position of assistant, you did not have any communications with Doboj or Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Those two centres were the only ones that existed and operated before the war. I had no communication with them. As for the others, they were just in the process of being established, and national security sectors were not established in them throughout my tenure. There was only one in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This entire system of communications that you spoke about while you were under-secretary, it never really came into operation during your tenure.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the national security sector is concerned, it did not come into operation. I don't know if that is also true of the public security sector. I can't say one way or another because I don't know. I just said that on one occasion Minister Lajic said they had bridged a gap on one line and it doesn't go through the Federation anymore.
