Now, which part of Republika Srpska it concerned, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That was precisely what I wanted to ask because I understood you as saying that communication lines went via the Federation and that was one of the major problems in communication; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Many intercepts are available here to this Tribunal and the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you say "Federation," you mean the Muslim/Croat Federation within the framework of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no other federation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now having clarified this, let us go back to our document. The next paragraph refers to the problem MUP was facing in pursuing the perpetrators of these criminal acts, and Stojan Zupljanin says that several thousand criminal cases have not been completed, there are no judges for criminal cases. Judges are intimidated. They are receiving threats. And in certain municipalities, like Bosanska Krupa, Donja Vas, Kupres, Derventa, courts are not working. And then Zupljanin goes on to say that hardened criminals are being released from prisons which has a great effect on the efforts to restore the rule of law and law enforcement. Mr. Skipina, do you agree with me that this is a serious problem which had a great impact on the functioning of the MUP at the time because practically whatever efforts the MUP was making had no effect?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And, in general, MUP is not the only one that's supposed to fight various kinds of crime. The prosecutor's office should also be involved. When they receive information that a crime has taken place, they could, on their own initiative, instruct the Ministry of the Interior to investigate, to find evidence, et cetera, but that happened very rarely. As far as courts are concerned, the situation was the same. A lot of personnel remained in the territory of the Federation, and most people were more concerned with finding a safe or better life in Montenegro, Serbia, or abroad. So it was the same problem. In the MUP, in the prosecution, in the judiciary, everywhere. But I agree with what is stated here; namely, that the problem was, indeed, very serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And whatever the police did, the -- when they detained someone, compiled a criminal report, filed it, if that person ran free again three days later, that certainly affected the work of the police and the morale of the citizens.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. It also affected the morale of the members of the MUP. If nothing is done to prosecute the person properly, it blunts the edge of the fight against crime and the morale of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that certain conclusions were made after this discussion but you are not aware of the procedure that followed. Let me just see if later, as an advisor to the minister, a period when you said you weren't doing anything, let me show you a document that reflects some conclusions of this meeting in Belgrade. It your tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it's Exhibit 2D25.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skipina, I don't think you saw this document before. It's from July 1992 from the Security Services Centre sent to public security stations, all of them, to the commands of the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, to the MUP for their information. Please look at page 3. It's page 4 in B/C/S, conclusion number 2. It's an order, in fact, an instruction. Stojan Zupljanin states explicitly after this meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, it's the next page, I think. Yes, that's the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In item 2 of this instruction, it says that public security stations may not receive or carry out any orders, decisions, conclusions, stances or similar by crisis or regional staffs or other legal entities, which have not been adopted according to established procedure and delivered in writing to public security stations and which do not relate to the jobs and tasks within the competence of the service or are not in accordance with the law and bylaws. This is one of the conclusions of the meeting. It's an instruction to the public security stations which are responsive to Crisis Staffs, that they should stop doing that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is consistent with the conclusions of that meeting of the collegium in -- from July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 6 regards the guarding of these detention centres. Stojan Zupljanin says that public security stations may not, without the approval of the centre, undertake to guard persons arrested by unauthorized persons, considering that these affairs do not fall within the purview of the service. This practically forbids the police to participate in the security in such centres.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it follows from the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that was one of the issues raised by Stojan Zupljanin at this meeting in Belgrade, on 11 July?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know when the time for the break is, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we were looking at that. I -- remembering that you indicated that you wouldn't be very brief, I wondered how close you are to finishing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have perhaps one more document to show to the witness and five questions on that document and that would be all. Some ten minutes, not more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... break and come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: here

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, I would like, while we are waiting for witness to come, just to correct the transcript regarding two 65 ter 266, it is not P1207, as stated in the transcript, so 65 ter 266 is Exhibit P1270. And for the clarity, just to repeat, that 65 ter 239 is P1269. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skipina, one other topic you haven't discussed during your evidence here, I have a question on that. While you were head of the National Security Service, were you aware of the existence of a group called Milos which was active in the AOR of Doboj and Banja Luka centres, and these were members of the National Security Service but went under the pseudonym of Milos, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the AOR of the Banja Luka CSB, I was aware of the existence of a parallel service called Tajfun. And later on, while I was advisor, I came to know that a Mice group or Mico's group was active in Teslic. And as for Milos, this is the first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at Exhibit P964, which is behind tab 3 in your folder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't particularly want to object, but if says he has never heard of Milos, I'm not sure how he can comment on this document, which is a Milos document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question only had to do with whether he ever received the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skipina, have a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to read it first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: While you were head of the National Security Service, you had received this document or a similar document bearing the signature Milos?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I ever received it, I would not have previously answered your question by saying that I was not aware of the name Milos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: From your subsequent contacts with Mr. Kesic, who was the head of the National Security Service in Banja Luka - in other words, of the Banja Luka national security centre - have you ever learnt of the formation of the group of Milos which dealt with operative work in the areas of the municipalities of Doboj and Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the first meeting in Belgrade where I got to know Mr. Kesic, he never discussed the matter. Later on I didn't have any discussions with Mr. Kesic on the issues regarding the service. This was in within the purview of the newly appointed head of the CSB Dragan Kijac. In other words, my answer is no, I had never discussed the existence of the Milos group with Mr. Kesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know a member of the National Security Service by the name of Predrag Radulovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I do know him. When I worked in the State Security Service of the Republican SUP, he became employed in Doboj in the State Security Centre there. I don't know if he ever went onto work for the Banja Luka NSS, and if so, when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were head of the service, did you receive any sort of report from him, such as an operative report or a report in general, a brief?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only -- it only would have been possible if he physically went through the corridor and turned it over to me, so throughout my term of office I never received any sort of report from Mr. Kesic or from --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Or from Radulovic, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from Radulovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skipina. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Skipina, before we give the floor to Mr. Cvijetic, I'd like to explore this last point that was made by Mr. Krgovic because I find it somehow odd that there would be a unit operating in your own house, in your own service, the SNB that was apparently operating without your knowledge. So my question to you is: Were you aware of the facts that there were several things that might have gone on in your one institution without you knowing of it, or does this come as a big surprise to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It came as an outright surprise to me. And if ever within the service, a subservice were to be formed, then in that situation, neither Mr. Kesic nor I could ever have been heads of our respective services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So how are we to -- to understand the evidence here? If I understand Mr. Krgovic correctly, he is assuming that the group Milos was working in the collection of evidence and intelligence in -- in the SNB, in the institution of which you were the chief. And you're now saying that you had no idea that this was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. I had no idea. But had I had normal communication, this would not have happened. There should not exist any sort of subgroup active within the National Security Service but operating outside of the rules of that service. It is illegal and unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Cvijetic cross-examines, on page 51, line 5, where the witness spoke about the parallel service called Typhoon, it's not actually spelled like the wind or the weather but it's Tajfun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Skipina, for the record, let me state that I am counsel, Slobodan Cvijetic, and I represent the Defence for Mr. Mico Stanisic. Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Initially I will be dealing with one period of your activity and work, which has been, in my view, gone through a bit too quickly since you are competent to deal with one topic in particular. As a member of the State Security Service, you dealt thoroughly with the phenomenon problem of nationalism on -- and when I say nationalism I mean Serb, Croat, and Muslim. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Of course, I'm referring to the pre-war period; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In your line of work related to nationalism, can you explain to us what your role was in the case involving Mr. Alija Izetbegovic? Just briefly, please. What your role in that was and what you did, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honours, I'm not at all sure how this is relevant to any of the issues that Your Honours are dealing with in this trial. I know that it's Mr. Cvijetic's thing that the historical background is of some importance. But at the moment I can't see that, and nor can I see how it's relevant whatever role this witness played in the investigation as to Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Where -- Mr. Cvijetic, could you assist us as to where are you going? This is wholly new, something that wasn't part of the Prosecution's case, and it, on the face of it, is not, as Ms. Korner said, relevant to any of the issues before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this will be just a couple of point from the historical context that I will tie in with the causes and reasons for the transformation and dissolution of the Ministry of Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the causes and reasons for this witness to leave Sarajevo, the causes and reasons for which many of the Serb personnel employed in the BH MUP did the same, et cetera. This is a topic that will shed light on what is relevant for this case. This is merely a brief introduction leading me to the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Two minutes, no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Sir, two minutes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1983, I was the key person in the State Security Service for documenting the counter constitutional activity of a group of Islamic fundamentalists headed by Alija Izetbegovic, Bekmir Omer [phoen], Hasan Cengic, and others. The platform of their activity was worked out by Mr. Izetbegovic in his book entitled: "The Islamic Declaration." And the inspiration for all of this was found by them in the successfully carried out Islamic revolution in Iran.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skipina, Mr. Izetbegovic was convicted and served his sentence. Was he being observed or surveilled by the State Security Service at the time as well?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I understand your question. When do you mean at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: While he was serving his sentence in Foca.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not being treated, although Munir Alibabic, the inspector of the State Security Service, did occasionally go to visit him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Based on these contacts and opinions, Mr. Izetbegovic's sentence was shortened considerably, as you will be aware. He did not serve the full sentence.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. He was sentenced to 14 years in prison and serve roughly six.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Shortly upon his release, he formed a party; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did the leadership of the party include the same individuals who shared his views before he was convicted?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same individuals who were involved in the 1983 case against Alija Izetbegovic took up the strategic positions in the party that he formed, the Party for Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will no longer dwell on the topic. We got two minutes to deal with it. Following the multi-party elections, the so-called division of power occurred among the three parties that won most of the votes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with my statement that the Serbian Democratic Party within this division of power, did come out short, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the general surprise of the population, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic insisted that he -- that they be given the Ministry of the Interior of all the ministries, since they won most of the votes. They were entitled to choose the ministry of their choosing. The other party that had the choice next was the Serbian Democratic Party, which opted for the Ministry of Agriculture. The third ranking party, the HDZ, took the Ministry of Defence. Even Mr. Kljuic himself stated for the television that they were grateful for -- to Mr. Karadzic for not opting for the Ministry of Defence. Mr. Karadzic opted for the Ministry of Agriculture. My conclusion about that issue today is that for this reason there are no Serbs in towns like Mostar, Zenica, Tuzla, and especially Sarajevo where many of them used to live earlier on but most of them now live in smaller places and their occupation is agriculture, which is what Mr. Karadzic had chosen for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that, in order for a state to be formed which is dominated by one peoples only, the key ministries were the Ministry of The interior, Ministry of Defence, and possibly the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. In times of war two key ministries are the Ministry of Defence and Ministry of the Interior. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, of course, means the art in negotiating with other countries and lobbying for positions and programmes you wish to implement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In order to achieve that goal, it was necessary to arm one's own people and, as for the Ministry of the Interior, the personnel of other ethnicities had to be either removed or marginalised; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how things actually developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This goes to the gist of my following question. How did this marginalisation come about, briefly, in the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Ministry of the Interior, there were certain problems in the SDA party as well. Namely, Mr. Izetbegovic insisted that he be the sole person appointing the minister of the interior. His candidate was the former minister of the interior, Mr. Besic. However, Fikret Abdic presented an obstacle because he received the most votes as a member of the Presidency, and he was supposed to be the first President of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was in favour of Alija Delimustafic, who was his candidate. There was a comprise in which Mr. Abdic gave up on being president in favour of Mr. Izetbegovic, and in return, Delimustafic was appointed minister of the interior. I can go on explaining this in more detail if needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That will already be my next question. How did the Serb personnel fair within the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDA kept most of the management personnel from the previous MUP, since they were professionals. On the other hand, the SDS used the best of Serb personnel, who existed at the time, gave up on them, I would say. It wasn't by their permission but due to the lack of their initiative, Sredoje Novic who -- the last person who was in charge of the state security sector who was supposed to be at the helm of the entire Yugoslav state sector as well as Momo Andzic [phoen] who was assistant minister for crime were removed, they were pensioned off or assigned to secretarial work in public security stations. Assistant Minister of the Interior, Mr. Hilmo Selimovic, did so by virtue of his decision. I also suffered under him significantly when I was pensioned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood, you worked on Mr. Hilmo Selimovic's case while you were still in the state security sector concerning his possible involvement in certain criminal activities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the state security sector we had received a document from the then-Republican Assembly containing information provided by certain employees in -- with respect to his activities at the time. He was, at that time, the general manager of the Sarajevo beer brewery. He was also a member of the Central Committee of the League of Communists at the time. I called Mr. Selimovic before my operatives came to see him in the brewery to check such information, telling him that it was my intention to send them to see, to verify that information. He asked Slobo, Please do not do that. Things are clear here. And I said to him, If it's true that there's nothing happening then we would submit a report to that effect, to the Assembly, which is only in your favour. I did send my operatives there, and they came across various indicia of embezzlement in terms of state-owned property. He came to see me in my office asking me to call off the investigation and the case, which I refused. When everything was completed, we compiles a report in the service, which we forwarded to the prosecutor's office, the Assembly and the city council because he was a member of the city council. After that report, he was excluded from the membership of the city council, but the prosecutor's office never followed up on that case because of things which went on behind the scenes. It simply retained the document but did nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So, in essence, he received a very important role in the Ministry of the Interior after the multi-party elections. He could even decide on personnel policy. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He made a purge in the Republican SUP, he drove away a lot of people, even Bosniaks if they had previously worked on the case of Alija Izetbegovic. Such people were, for example, Borisa Delic, who was my deputy. He's a Bosniak and holds law degree and has perfect command of two languages. He appointed him to a position in Han Pijesak, which is 80 kilometres away. Of course, he refused because he hailed from the city. When he refused, he asked him what information he had on him so that he could prosecute me. My deputy, Mr. Delic told him he had nothing to share with him about me and then Selimovic asked him to go to see me so that he would tell me that eventually I would get arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: During the purge, the Serb personnel faired very poorly.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In my personal opinion as a policeman, since I knew a lot of those people, people who did not fulfil the needs of such positions were appointed to the positions of those who had previously been sent away.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 60, line 14, it seems that the witness's answer figures as a question, so we have the answer continuing. This is not a new question. Could we please show a document to the witness, which is 1D118, and with the assistance of the usher, could we please provide these hard copies to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skipina, this is already in evidence. It was compiled by employees of the state security sector of Serb ethnicity. The title speaks for itself. It is in your tab 1. There's no need for you to follow it on the screen. Please see what the title is and then we'll go to the contents. It is quite a voluminous document, but we will refer to it briefly only.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the first page, please, now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, Mr. Skipina, the last sentence it says that this service has so far been the inclusive function of the SDA and the HDZ for the following reasons, and you have already addressed those. In the second paragraph it is stated that the SDS, that is to say, the Serbs got the fifth and sixth administration in the services or in the sectors. In the fourth paragraph it is stated that the SDS lost the second person in the State Security Service, the position which should have been assigned to Mr. Nedjo Vlaski, and I believe you are familiar with that situation. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are. For a while Dragan Devedlaka was supposed to have been appointed and then Nedjo Vlaski was the next candidate, but neither of them was appointed to that position which apparently ceased to exist at a late point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to the next page. There are various facts and further evidence of this process of marginalising Serb personnel. On page 5 in the last paragraph, it is stated that only Serb politicians and staff were being wire-tapped. Is it true that the service was used to wire-tap only Serb personnel?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, unless you have a transcript of that service concerning Kljuc, Izetbegovic, and others, then you can conclude for yourself who were the subjects of wire-tapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: There's also a mention made of the withdrawal of equipment from Sarajevo and other centres. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not privy to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I believe we can agree on the following conclusion: That one of the methods of creating a state following one's own interest was to have control of the Ministry of the Interior. Am I correct in assuming that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could another method be also creating one's own army inside the Ministry of the Interior or turning it into a party army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you expand the reserve force of the police to levels which are extraordinary, then one could arrive at such a conclusion too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Hilmo Selimovic during a single night used to issue three -- up to 300 appointments or decisions by which people were employed in the Ministry of the Interior or made part of the reserve force and who were mainly Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with any figures, but I know of the existence of such orders. I learned of that through my contacts with the operatives whose superior I used to be. And these people were Serbs, Muslim, and Croats who held me in high regard as a person who had formally been a part of the management structure, and they shared this information with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in 1991, the SDA, illegally so to speak, or contrary to the rules, and that they went beyond the police school in Vrace in order to send certain personnel to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that, but I do know that the key person in charge of the functioning of the MUP on behalf of the SDA was Hasan Cengic who was tried alongside Mr. Izetbegovic, and such a person was in charge of all MUP policy, and you can only imagine what such a MUP would look like afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain what you also wanted to say about Mr. Cengic. You said he was an Imam?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a -- part of the clergy. He was equivalent to a cleric in other religious communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within the context of this topic, for ease of reference, could we please have P424, MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Which is your tab 2. This is what we have just discussed. Before you is one of similar lists, of which which we have several. In this case, there were 463 members sent for training to Croatia. The document was signed by Hasan Cengic himself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The cover page where it says: List. Do you know who was the secretary of that party?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I wonder where we are going with this. I believe the witness has told us that he was unaware of the fact that the SDA was sending people to Croatia for military training sort of outside the normal procedures. So isn't that the end of this topic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was about to make the same objection. Unless the witness has seen the document before, is familiar with any of its contents, this is leading us nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, then we don't have it correct in the transcript. I seem to have heard the witness that he was familiar with that type of activity of the party but that he was not familiar with the figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you know whether any people were sent for training to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I knew or that I had heard that policemen were sent for training to Croatia, but I don't know anything else. I just know that they were sent for military training to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yesterday, in response to one of the questions by Ms. Korner, you mentioned a specific fact linked to this subject; namely, the arming of the Muslim population in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... page number, please, of where the question is in transcript, from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking of the document that I was about to show. He was talking about a document which deals with the arming, and I'm going to show the document now. It is 1D --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you said yesterday in an answer to a question by me. You said he gave an answer, and I'm asking you what question, what answer, on what page of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain. Mr. Skipina was saying yesterday that he had interrogated a person who had been detained, and he was the key organiser of the arming activities in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's on page 8304. And that person made a statement about the arming activities. It was videotaped, and it was even broadcast publicly. That is the part of the witness's evidence I'm referring to. Can we place 1D03-2306 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just correct the transcript, the page is 8305, line 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skipina, it's the last document in your folder, tab 25, I think. Is that the person you mentioned yesterday, Senad Emic. This is his statement. Sorry, Senad Memic. And if you leaf through, you will find his handwritten statement. Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. But his full name is Senahid. Senahid Memic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is that the person -- and, in fact, it's written in his own statement, written in longhand, Senahid Memic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the person I mentioned yesterday. He was caught with five or six different false IDs in Serbian names, among other things. He had a membership card of the SDS party. He had passes to different institutions, agencies, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Look at the printed part of his statement. He names practically all the key persons from the SDA party as being involved in the arming. And you -- you know all this. You don't have to read.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can both read it, and I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: He goes on to say, through which channels the arms were purchased, how they were distributed. He mentions another cleric, a Muslim Imam in Zagreb. It's on page 2. It should be the first paragraph on page 2, Sefer Omerbasic, the Zagreb mosque Imam?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know -- he was under surveillance by the State Security Service of Croatia before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And then follows his handwritten statement, the same text as the printed version. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Skipina, did you use any illegal methods to coerce this person into writing this statement such as beating or anything else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a normal interview. I was even criticised by my colleagues in the police force when I decided to exchange this man. Mr. Bakir Alispahic, for instance, told me, Why don't we prosecute him? I said, Let's play it down, we are not going to win anything if we try him and convict him. Let him -- let him go over, but let us keep all the documents. And, indeed, I had him exchanged in the first round of exchanges that I organised with the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just after -- for the transcript, the -- the second sentence in this last passage is the beginning of the answer. Currently it is all recorded as my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: To finish with this document, Mr. Skipina, you confirmed the authenticity of this document, you are aware of it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe all the requirements are met to admit this document, and I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm happy if it is admitted as to -- this is what the witness says was said in this statement, but not as to the truth of its contents, if I can draw that distinction. If it's being -- if the reason is because it's going to be said, so that Mr. Cvijetic understands, that, therefore, what is said in this statement is the truth and the Trial Chamber should accept it as the truth, well, then I'd object. If it is simply being admitted to show this is what was said in this statement by this man, Memic, then I have no objection. But I would object to any attempt to address the Chamber on the basis of what is said in there is true. The proper course would be to call Mr. Memic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, are you tendering this for the fact of the document or the truth of its contents?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the Rules of this Tribunal, circumstantial evidence is allowed. But the point here is in the authenticity of the document, and the Prosecution, of course, will not miss a chance to question the allegations made therein. But let me ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Was it your impression and did you have any other corroborative information for the allegations made here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically yes, but I would have to re-read it to refresh my memory as to the specific facts. But, in general terms, that's what I spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe all the conditions are met, Your Honours, for admitting this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... question that I asked earlier? The mere fact that this document exists, in other words, the piece of paper that you're putting before the Tribunal, or are you seeking to rely on what the document contains as being accurate and, therefore, evidence on which you're relying? Because if it is the latter, then -- then you come square up against the objection Ms. Korner articulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both, Your Honour. The witness is the one who took this statement, not a third party. The witness took this statement himself, and he can answer both your questions. Namely, that the document is authentic and that he had the impression that the statements made by the interviewee were correct and that he had other information to corroborate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What Mr. Cvijetic is trying to do is to get around the provisions of Rule 92. If he is trying to rely on the statement for evidence of the truth of the contents, he has two options: One is he calls the witness viva voce as part of his case; the second is he obtains a 92 ter statement saying that this is true or I suppose -- he cannot have it in on this basis and argue that its contents are true. The best he can hope to do at this stage is have it as a statement that apparently this witness took.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry to interrupt, but Mr. Smith has kindly brought something to my attention. This statement is 17 pages long in B/C/S, and we've got a translation of three pages, so it's not even properly translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In order not to delay today's proceedings, what I would do is have the document marked, and we move on. Mr. Cvijetic, did you take Ms. Korner's point, that what we have is a partial translation of a document, so the Chamber and, of course, the side opposite has a difficulty in addressing -- in the Chamber's part, comprehending it; for the -- for the OTP's part, in terms of addressing it. So in order not to delay today's proceedings, let's move on ... for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, if I may be of assistance, there is a misunderstanding between Ms. Korner's understanding and the facts in this particular document. The documents consists of the typewritten statement typed by this witness or somebody from the MUP who was taking the statement and the handwritten -- the very same statement of the person who gave the statement, so it's in handwritten form. The person, this Senahid Memic, wrote it with his own hand and then it was retyped. So there is no point of -- of translating twice the very same content. That is why the translation consists of only the typewritten document and the handwritten document just to prove the accuracy and truthfulness of this statement because it was signed and written by this particular person, and that is why it is a full -- a full translation of the contents of this document. It's just that it's basically two documents but with the same content. I hope I was of assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I understand, and with that explanation, the position that the Chamber takes is that it would be admitted, and counsel are alerted that the argument and the appropriate time would be a question as to what weight to give to it. Because obviously in terms of the truth to which it purports to speak, because it is not the witness's statement and the maker, the effective maker is -- is apparently not being called as a witness, then there is an argument to be advanced as to how much weight the Chamber should give it at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, so I just understand, Your Honours are admitting it as an exhibit but will not - I hope I have got this right - but will not accept that its contents are true in the absence of the maker being called or a statement to that effect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No. I -- I think that you overstated the position, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As I understand the rules of the Tribunal -- the rules of evidence applying to this Tribunal, hearsay evidence may be admitted in certain circumstances. The particular document is being tendered through the witness -- through the witness on the stand who recorded it. As with any other witness performing such a function he is hardly ever able to testify to the truth of the contents, and the argument may be made that having regard to the fact that the witness is giving evidence why do we need the document, but for the sake of completeness - I can think of no other appropriate word - we would allow the document in. But it is obvious that because of the -- what it is and how it came to be made, there is a -- then the Defence at the appropriate stage is making its argument, they would appreciate that the -- that it is for them to persuade the Chamber to give it the -- the weight which they would undoubtedly seek to have it given by the fact that they were seeking to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, Your Honours, can I -- I agree. It is quite a difficult point. But Rule 92, which governs the admission -- I see Mr. Pantelic wants to say something, but can I just finish. Rule 92, which governs the admission of written statements and transcripts in lieu of oral testimony, says that factors against admitting evidence in the form of a written statement or transcript include but are not limited to whether there's an overriding public interest in the evidence being presented orally. A party objecting can demonstrate that its nature and source renders it unreliable, and, three, there are any other factors. So, Your Honours, which -- there is a difference between admitting it, because this witness says this is the statement I took, and giving any weight at all in these circumstances to the truth of its contents. I -- appreciating that hearsay is admissible, we would submit and this is -- I don't agree. I don't want to take up too much time, but we would submit that statements of this nature, in the light of what you have heard about similar statements of this nature, to admit it as true would be contrary to the spirit of the rules. That's our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much Your Honours. It's from my point of view issue of certain importance. I think my learned friend, Ms. Korner, is not right with respect to the structure of that problem. Point number one is that the witness here was an official professional police officer who was in capacity to get this statement from -- from a suspect or from a person. That's point number one. Point number two is that if we are going to follow the pattern that my learned friend, Ms. Korner, is suggesting us here, then, in thousands of various occasions where we have to evaluate the -- the -- the -- the documents in -- in particular court proceedings that we already admitted or many other statements with regard to the facts occurred as a background of certain event, et cetera, et cetera, then we shall be in very serious problem. My humble advice would be now to permit -- to my learned friend, Mr. Cvijetic, to see and check with -- with -- with witness, is there any other corroborative evidence or documents or any other source that gave the right to this witness to conclude that this was a truthful statement. Then we are going to second point. I mean, the second part of the game. If Ms. Korner is challenging this evidence, facts, all other relevant issues, then she is very welcome to bring the person in question, the suspect, or to obtain from him by the way of deposition or 92 bis statement, relevant statement of that witness and then, only then, this Trial Chamber will be in the situation to give a weight, certain weight to the evidence, to the exhibit. So I think my proposition is constructive and maybe we should permit our learn friend, Mr. Cvijetic, to find a proper way to -- to -- to get the personal knowledge and -- and practically evidence from this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I -- I don't think that Rule 92 has anything to do with this problem. Nobody until now is introducing the gentleman that wrote this -- this statement as a witness. That's what Rule 92 is about, it's about witness statements. Nobody says that this gentleman, Memic, or whatever his name is, is a witness. It's a document that is standard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honours, that's exactly the point I'm trying to make. Your Honour has actually hit it in one. The document itself I perfectly accept if it is going in purely for the basis that it is a document apparently seen or taken by this witness, and this is what is recorded in the document. What -- the Defence are trying to go one further and say that you, the Trial Chamber, should accept this -- the contents of this statement as the statement of Mr. Memic as the truth. So they are, in fact, attempting to make this man a witness without calling him. Your Honours, that's the only -- otherwise how could they possibly do this otherwise? They can't call Mr. Memic, and they know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, with respect, it is. They're trying to make this man, what he said in this statement, they are saying you should accept as true. In other words, he -- what you are being asked to say, this is a witness as to the truth of what's contained in this document. There is a real difference between the document going in as a document. This is what's recorded in the document as opposed to without hearing the witness, without any of the Rule 92 safe-guards, that's the point. You should accept what is in the statement. So it is trying to get round Rule 92 by this method. I can see Your Honour is not convinced but if you think about it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear all that, Ms. Korner. I heard a document that was tendered and you're trying to make a distinction and what is tendered, the document or the statement, the truth or -- that's a distinction we until now never made.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... but, Your Honour ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... another document come in and all the rest is weight.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no. But, Your Honour, this is slightly different, and this has happened before that these so-called confessions made by people in the custody of RS municipal are being put in in order to show you that what was in those contents -- sorry, what is contained in the statement are true. Now that is not a proper way of dealing with these matters, and it is an attempt to get round Rule 92. Because otherwise these witnesses should be called or statements taken from them under the circumstances of how they came to make the statements. Now the onus is being put on the Prosecution to call these witnesses. We have the difficulty firstly of whether we can find the witnesses, which in one case we can't, or whether you will allow us to put in extra evidence to counter this. Mr. Pantelic has invited us to do that. But we say that if the Defence wish to rely on these statements as being true then they have two options: One is to call the maker; or secondly, to obtain the proper certification under Rule 92. And, I'm sorry, it's standard stuff that -- that -- I say -- that if a statement is -- is put in without the maker being called there has to be good reason as to why the maker is not being called.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And Ms. Korner have a right for her theory, but I protest for the using word of so-called confessions. If that's a part of theory, it's okay. But so-called confessions in this particular case and other cases it is well, well beyond the proper standards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Krgovic, you wanted to make a point?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I think Mr. Zecevic will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm thankful for Ms. Korner for her explanation. The only thing that now strucks [sic] me -- I'm returning a bit back in the case. We have a decision by the Honourable Trial Chamber on the assistance of the Office of the Prosecutor concerning the intercepts. Now are we to understand that the intercepts, the documents have been admitted only as documents without -- without this -- the allegation of truthfulness of -- of the contents of these documents, because, in this case, we also did not have the person who created these documents. Now, this is a -- I don't know -- I'm -- I'm just rather putting my observation on the issue and we intend to deal with the -- with the -- with Your Honours' ruling in -- in our written submission. But I'm just putting -- putting this observation now before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, Ms. Korner, gentlemen, thank you. It is 1.45. It is time that we take the adjournment for today. The document as tendered may be admitted and marked and no doubt at some point we would seek to be persuaded by Ms. Korner that the content should be wholly disregarded. So we take the adjournment until tomorrow morning at 9.00, I believe, we are still in this courtroom. And I would remind the witness of what I said yesterday about not discussing the matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
